taxonomyNote: Recently split from C. viridis (Pook 2000; Ashton & de Queiroz 2001; Douglas 2002); some older sources treat it as a subspecies of C. viridis. NatureServe notes the boundary in the Four Corners region needs clarification.
fieldMarks: Horny rattle on the tail tip; head much broader than the neck
Heat-sensing pit on each side of the face; vertical pupil in bright light
Colour from light tan or pink to black with large blotches on back and sides, banded tail
Light stripe from behind the eye to the mouth corner; rarely exceeds 3.3 ft
behavior: Rattle can sound for minutes; burrowing owls and gopher snakes make hissing that resembles it
Diet mainly small mammals, also birds, lizards and rarely amphibians
In British Columbia gravid females generally did not feed
Pregnant females may congregate near winter dens
habitat: Shrubby coastal dunes to timberline, basins, canyons and open mountain forest; uses mammal burrows and crevices.
range: Southern British Columbia south to central Baja California and east to the Rocky Mountains.

lookalikes.name: Prairie rattlesnake
lookalikes.howToTell: Former parent species; occupies the plains east of the Rockies from southern Alberta and Saskatchewan.

lookalikes.name: Gopher snake
lookalikes.howToTell: Makes a hiss that can sound like rattling but has no rattle.
